Project Description — AstroGuard

AstroGuard is an AI-powered astronaut health-monitoring system designed to help monitor astronauts' physiological conditions throughout space missions. It focuses on four major health systems: cardiovascular, cognitive, immune, and musculoskeletal, while considering NASA's five major spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. The system works by organizing astronaut health measurements, analyzing historical changes, establishing personal baselines, forecasting future health indicators, and identifying unusual measurement patterns that may require further medical review. It presents this information through an interactive dashboard where users can explore astronaut profiles, health measurements, historical trends, and machine learning predictions.

Our solution combines real NASA research data with synthetic astronaut data. We integrated two datasets from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), OSD-569 (Complete Blood Count) and OSD-575 (Comprehensive Metabolic Panel), from the Inspiration4 mission. We extracted biomarkers such as white blood cell count (WBC), neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages, and serum calcium. We also calculated the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and combined compatible measurements from four astronauts across seven preflight and postflight collection timepoints, producing 28 aligned observations. Since real astronaut health datasets are limited and do not provide enough continuous measurements for our forecasting requirements, we generated a separate synthetic dataset of 30 simulated astronauts with 15 baseline days and 70 mission days. This dataset was used to train four LightGBM models that forecast resting heart rate, cognitive reaction time, NLR, and bone-density drift over seven days. We also used an Isolation Forest algorithm to identify unusual patterns in multiple health measurements. Importantly, the real NASA measurements are kept separate from the synthetic training data and are used for research-based comparisons rather than training the forecasting models.

To develop the system, we used Python as our main programming language, with Pandas and NumPy for data processing and numerical calculations, LightGBM for forecasting, Scikit-learn for anomaly detection and model validation, and Joblib for saving and loading trained models. We built the backend using FastAPI and Uvicorn, which process data, execute models, and provide results through REST APIs. The frontend uses React and Vite to present information through an interactive dashboard. We also used GitHub for version control and collaboration, and Pytest for backend testing. No custom medical hardware or wearable device was developed; the prototype works with research datasets and simulated measurements.

The creativity of AstroGuard comes from combining multiple health systems, machine learning, real spaceflight research, and NASA's five-hazard framework in one platform rather than monitoring individual measurements separately. We also considered several important factors during development, including the limited availability of real astronaut data, differences in measurement units and collection schedules, missing measurements, data reliability, and the need to distinguish actual NASA observations from simulated predictions. We designed the system to report data limitations and treat unusual patterns as indicators for human review rather than medical diagnoses. Our intended impact is to support more organized astronaut health monitoring, help mission personnel recognize potentially concerning changes earlier, and contribute to the development of more reliable health-monitoring approaches for future long-duration space missions.
